1.title: Black-box pen tests on Replit
1.author: Alexandre Cuoci
1.description:
Replit enables you to build apps to create and launch apps that hold real customer data within a day.

Before coding agents, a full pre-launch security review required procuring a pen test from a vendor that would cost thousands, and weeks of back-and-forth. A penetration (”pen”) test is a safe, authorized mock cyberattack that helps you fix security flaws before bad hackers find them.

As we have democratized software creation, we have also sought to democratize securing it. A new generation of creators needs to ensure their apps are hardened against attackers, who look at apps built with AI as an opportunity as a potential opportunity.

Our existing scans have an agent read your code and look for patterns that tend to be dangerous. That catches a lot, and it runs every time you build.

But a malicious hacker doesn’t see your code. Instead, they open your app and start poking around to find any doors you might have left unlocked. It’s a totally different way of searching that leads to different results. The gap between these two approaches is where most actual break-ins happen: even if nothing in the code looks wrong, the app might still hand over data it shouldn’t.

Your built-in security team

3.title: Govern Replit at scale
3.author: The Replit Team
3.description:
New Admin API, Audit Logs, and Workspace Settings give organizations more insight and flexibility into how they adopt AI with Replit.



Replit helps teams turn ideas into working software quickly. Most companies start with a handful of builders and a few prototypes. Then it works, and it spreads: more teams, more projects, more software running in production.

That shift creates work for a specific group of people. As AI tools spread across a company: IT, procurement, and admin teams absorb the cost. They field permission requests, run access reviews, make policy decisions tool by tool, and answer questions about what is running where. The requests pile up faster than those teams can grow.

We’re announcing a set of updates that are available today and will continuously be updated in the coming weeks. These updates are aimed at supporting enterprise adoption of AI, built to take that work off admins' plates:

Comprehensive Audit Logs: More than 50 events across deployments, identity, secrets, and agent activity, with native streaming to your SIEM. Available today.

5.title: The feature was fine. So why did users keep hiding it?
5.author: SoYoon Park (DR. PARK)
5.description:
The retention killer that never shows up in a requirements doc.

The room was in Seoul, quiet except for the hum of the air conditioner. Behind the one-way mirror, product planners sat with notebooks, in the years before K-beauty shook the world. Then one sentence broke the silence.

“If my boyfriend gives me this brand as a gift, that’s his way of telling me he wants to break up.”

Every participant in the room nodded, as if on cue. The second sentence hit even harder.

“The lipstick has incredible color payoff. But I take just the product out and transfer it into a Chanel case before I carry it.”

Lipstick is the one cosmetic that lives in public view. Its case isn’t packaging. It’s an accessory, in the same category as a watch or a wallet. A Chanel case was the smallest unit of luxury she could actually own, and the cheapest tool available for defending her identity in front of other people. She hadn’t rejected the product: she loved the color payoff and used it every day. What she rejected was the signal the brand sent to everyone watching. With her own hands, she’d taken a knife to it and cut function clean away from identity.

Fabricio Teixeira has made a related point about out-of-box experience: what happens after purchase is still part of the product experience, and physical touchpoints continue carrying the brand story. MISSHA showed what happens when that story clashes with the user’s own identity.

Translate that into product terms: core feature satisfaction, off the charts. Repurchase and referral intent, on the floor. Run the usability tests, mine the open-ended NPS responses, and the reason never surfaces. It’s the wall every planner eventually hits, staring at a requirements doc that has nothing wrong with it.

Same spec sheet, completely different retention.

MISSHA opened the “roadshop” category at a startling $3 a product, and grew from a single Korean brand into one now sold across more than 40 countries. LANEIGE sat in the same affordable range, but it occupied a completely different place in consumers’ minds. An Amorepacific brand now sold through Sephora in more than twenty countries, it was never expensive, but never embarrassing to pull out in public either.

The price gap between the two brands was negligible, and their ingredient lists were close enough that no spec comparison would explain the difference. Then latecomers arrived at the same price point and layered on identity. One built a store experience like a princess’s dressing room; another filled every touchpoint with a consistent nature-first message. That’s where the crack started.

The question in every product review meeting was always the same: “What feature do we add to lift retention?” The question itself was wrong. The spec deck, packed card after card, was missing nothing. The requirements doc, by design, was never built to hold the axis of “how do I look to other people, using this?”

Why identity feedback never makes it into a spec.

The raw voices from the repositioning research didn’t pull punches.

Hearing “tacky” and “embarrassing” puts a planner in a bind. A usability problem, like “I can’t find the button,” has a clear owner and a clear fix. An identity problem has no owner. It’s scattered across the logo, the copy, the tone of voice, and the store lighting. It’s impossible to cut into a single Scrum ticket.

Then came the sentence that flipped the table.

“Among affordable brands, Laneige is one I can take out in front of my boyfriend without embarrassment, but MISSHA is not.”

No standard benchmarking data, no quantitative metric, will ever catch that gap. Delivering “this looks tacky” straight to the executives who built the brand made for a silent debrief room. But the project succeeded for one reason: feedback nobody could quantify still got put at the top of the roadmap, instead of filed away in an appendix. The harder step was organizational: leadership chose not to defend the brand against the research. They treated the discomfort as evidence to work with, rather than something to explain away.

Launched in 2000, MISSHA was one of Korea’s original affordable beauty pioneers, helping establish the one-brand-shop model that became a defining part of early K-beauty.

The axis missing from the priority matrix.

One useful way to translate Jennifer Aaker’s brand-personality theory into UX terms is to think about two axes at once.

The function axis: does this solve my problem?
The identity axis: what does using this say about me to other people?

The identity mismatch can run in two directions: who users believe they are and who they want to become. MISSHA fit neither. In those sessions, it represented a version of the self they were trying to leave behind.

The requirements docs, feature specs, and competitive matrices we write cover almost only the first axis. The second gets waved off with “brand or design will handle it.”

But the real switch that flips churn is the second axis. Function can be excellent, and if the identity score is low, users hide the product: no screenshots, no mentions on social, quietly buried two pages deep in a home-screen folder. When the identity axis is strong, users will happily tolerate real functional flaws.

This pattern is playing out right now. A KPMG and University of Melbourne study of 48,000 respondents across 47 countries found that 57% of employees admit to hiding their AI use at work. In a controlled Atlassian experiment, identical work was rated far lazier the moment it was disclosed as AI-assisted. High satisfaction and concealed usage: the same structure as a lipstick moved into a Chanel case.

How a single raw sentence rewrote the roadmap.

MISSHA’s recovery started right there. The repositioning concept, “Bold Beauty,” came straight out of those sessions, and every touchpoint was rebuilt around a single ideal-user image: a confident career woman living on her own terms. Trace any decision back far enough and it lands on a sentence a consumer actually said out loud. Not a metric. A sentence was the basis for the roadmap.

3 actionable steps for your next sprint

  1. Add an identity axis to the priority matrix. Next to the impact-effort matrix, ask one more question: does this feature reinforce the user’s ideal self-image? Nielsen Norman Group’s State of UX 2026 makes a related point: as design systems and standardization make competent UI easier to produce, surface-level interface quality is becoming less of a differentiator. That makes the identity axis harder to dismiss as “just branding.”
  2. Add “did you hide it?” to your churn interviews. “Why did you stop using this?” only returns predictable feature complaints. Add: “Have you ever told a coworker or friend you use this app?” and “Have you ever screenshotted this screen to share it with someone?” If usability is fine but people are reluctant to show it off, that service is quietly sitting on a time bomb.
  3. Put unquantified sentences on the roadmap agenda. We’re in an era where AI summarizes thousands of VOC entries in seconds. But Nielsen Norman Group’s research on AI-generated review summaries found that even well-designed summaries fail to answer the specific question a user actually cared about — customers kept clicking back to individual reviews to find the exact detail the summary had smoothed over. A sentence like “I’m embarrassed to use this in front of my boyfriend” gets reduced, in the summary, to a flat line like “brand image needs improvement.” What flips the table isn’t a summarized chart. It’s a user’s raw sentence.

Closing

Identity isn’t an extra line item to hand off to the brand team. It has to come into the product document as its own axis. Leave it out, and even the most polished feature eventually becomes replaceable.

Picture the product you’re building right now. Does the user proudly pull it up in public, or quietly bury it two pages deep in a folder?

This article draws on consumer research the author advised on during a Korean beauty brand’s revitalization project, and reflects participant perceptions within a specific research context and point in time.

Dr. Park uncover unspoken consumer needs and turn them into new product concepts, brand strategies, and market opportunities.

6.title: AI adoption and the slow erosion of design idealism
6.author: Michael Buckley
6.description:
How years of client work, deadlines, and professional practice reshape a designer’s relationship with emerging technology.

I was having lunch with a couple of friends the other day. Both are designers around my age, in their early forties, and have been working in the profession for roughly as long as I have, about 20 years. As you might expect, our conversation eventually drifted toward AI.

Both of them talked extensively about how they have integrated AI into their workflows, which I found particularly interesting because they work in somewhat different corners of the design profession. One is an SVP of Design focused primarily on high-level UX strategy. The other freelances across graphic design, branding, and packaging.

The conversation got me thinking about what actually makes a designer more likely to embrace AI. My recent transition from industry to academia has exposed me to two very different ways of thinking about both the role AI should play in design and the role it is already playing in practice.

The assumption that did not survive

When AI first appeared, I assumed younger designers would be the first to adopt it. After all, they were practically handed an iPad at birth, while I still remember the sound of a dial-up modem and typing text messages on the numeric keypad of a flip phone. It seemed reasonable to assume that a generation raised alongside digital technology would be more comfortable integrating AI into its workflow than designers who built their careers long before these tools existed.

However, the more I paid attention to who was actually embracing AI, the less convincing the generational explanation became. Some of the most enthusiastic adopters in my professional circle have 15-plus years of experience.

In contrast, some of the strongest resistance I’ve encountered has come from people less immersed in the day-to-day realities of professional design practice, including students, academics, part-time designers, and those still early in their careers.

The theory I can’t stop testing

Here’s what I have landed on, and I want to be clear that this is anecdotal, not a study. I think a designer’s willingness to adopt AI has less to do with age or technical literacy and more to do with how many years of professional experience have tempered their expectations of how design operates in the real world.

I think most designers enter the profession with a somewhat romantic view of what design will be. Whether it’s artistic expression, problem-solving, innovation, or the desire to create something meaningful, there’s usually an idealized version of design that attracts us to the field in the first place. That idealism is often enough to carry us through design school and into our first jobs.

And then the profession introduces itself.

The slow erosion of the dream

Nobody warns you how quickly deadlines, revision cycles, stakeholder opinions, and budget constraints begin to reshape your understanding of what good design actually is. You stop asking, “Is this beautiful?” and start asking, “Can this ship by Thursday?” You learn that the client’s brother-in-law somehow has an opinion about the logo. You discover that many organizations that claim to value design really see it as a business function that happens to involve aesthetics.

That does not mean designers stop caring. I still care deeply about the work I put my name on. But somewhere along the way, priorities began to shift. Artistic purity used to dominate the conversation. Today, it’s one factor among many, sitting alongside efficiency, consistency, scalability, and the ability to deliver quality work without working myself into the ground.

I think this is where many designers become a little more jaded—although that word probably carries more negativity than I intend. What really changes is their relationship with the work itself. The romanticism begins to fade, and design becomes less about preserving an ideal and more about solving problems within real-world constraints.

That shift, at least in my experience, is the real dividing line. Not age or technical literacy. It’s about how much of your original idealism has survived contact with the industry.

AI walks right into that gap

If you still think of design primarily through the lens of creativity, craftsmanship, or personal expression, AI can feel threatening. It is a machine reaching into a space that feels deeply personal and asking whether part of your creative process can be automated.

But if years of professional practice have already taught you that much of your job involves solving problems under messy real-world conditions rather than pursuing pure self-expression, AI does not feel like an intrusion at all. It feels like another tool.

I don’t think the designers who have embraced AI are less passionate about their work. I think many of them have relocated that passion. It no longer lives in the repetitive execution of design tasks. Instead, it lives further upstream in strategy, concept development, systems thinking, and deciding what should be built in the first place.

Once that transition happens, it’s much easier to allow a tool to handle parts of the process that were never the source of your professional fulfillment.

Not all design work benefits from AI equally

There’s another variable that I think matters just as much, and that’s the type of design work you actually do.

AI doesn’t provide the same value across every area of the profession, and pretending otherwise is one reason these conversations become so polarized. Work that is structured, information-dense, iterative, or constrained by usability requirements, such as UX flows, design systems, and documentation-heavy interfaces, tends to benefit enormously from AI. That kind of work rewards speed and consistency, and AI happens to be very good at both.

Work built around experimentation, individual expression, and aesthetic exploration is a different story. A designer developing a distinctive visual language isn’t necessarily searching for a faster workflow. They are searching for ideas that haven’t been explored before. AI often struggles in those situations, not because it’s technically incapable, but because efficiency is not the primary goal.

That might explain why conversations about AI often seem so incoherent when designers argue about it online. A UX designer optimizing a checkout flow and an illustrator developing a personal visual style may both call themselves designers, but they’re not doing the same job. They’re not solving the same problems, and they’re certainly not evaluating AI through the same lens.

Students, early-career designers, academics, agency professionals, in-house UX teams, and working artists all operate under different conditions, with different incentives, and with very different relationships to the romantic idea of design.

Playing the cynic, on purpose

I will admit there is something a little uncomfortable about this theory because it challenges many of the assumptions we make about AI adoption. We often assume that designers who embrace AI are the most technologically fluent, the most adaptable, or the most willing to experiment with new tools. I’m not convinced that’s what’s happening.

After enough years of client calls, stakeholder meetings, unrealistic deadlines, budget constraints, and endless revision cycles, a tool that promises to remove some of that friction doesn’t necessarily feel like a threat. Design is still meaningful, but your identity is no longer completely wrapped up in the craft itself.

That’s not necessarily a depressing conclusion. Plenty of designers make that transition willingly and become better, calmer, and more effective professionals as a result. But it does suggest that we should be more careful about the stories we tell ourselves regarding who embraces AI and who rejects it.

I don’t think it’s really about intelligence, age, or technological sophistication. I think it’s about how much of our original idealism has survived contact with professional practice and whether we have made peace with the reality that, however much we love design, it’s also a job.
